title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls & Code Smells 🕳️
description: Steer clear of eval, bare variables, backticks, and insecure temporary files.

slides.title: The `eval` Monster 👹
slides.content:
## Avoid Unless Absolutely Necessary

`eval` forces the shell to parse its arguments as a command, which can execute arbitrary code if the input is uncontrolled.

```bash
cmd="rm -rf /"
eval $cmd   # disaster if $cmd comes from user
```
Instead, use arrays or direct command invocations. If you must use eval, sanitise input meticulously.

quizData.question: Using `eval` on unsanitised user input is safe because Bash handles quoting automatically.
quizData.explanation: `eval` can execute arbitrary code; it's a major security risk if input isn't strictly controlled.

slides.title: Unquoted Variable Expansion 💣
slides.content:
## We've Said It Before...

`for file in $files` loops over word‑split items. `[ $var = "yes" ]` fails if `$var` is empty. **Always quote**. There is almost never a good reason to leave expansions unquoted.

slides.title: Unquoted in Test
slides.codeSnippet:
if [ $name = "admin" ]; then   # BAD if $name empty -> [ = admin ] -> syntax error
# correct:
if [ "$name" = "admin" ]; then

slides.title: Insecure Temporary Files 📂
slides.content:
## Use `mktemp`

Never create temp files with a predictable name like `/tmp/myapp.$$`. This is vulnerable to symlink attacks.

Always use `mktemp`:
- `mktemp` creates a unique file with 600 permissions.
- `mktemp -d` creates a temp directory.
- Trap EXIT to clean up.

slides.title: Safe Temp File
slides.codeSnippet:
tmpfile=$(mktemp) || exit 1
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT
# work with $tmpfile

quizData.question: What command creates a unique temporary file safely?
quizData.explanation: `mktemp` generates a unique filename and creates the file with secure permissions.

slides.title: Backticks vs `$( )` 🧹
slides.content:
## Modern Syntax Wins

Backticks (`` ` ``) are deprecated. They make nesting awkward and are easily confused with single quotes. Use `$( )` instead.

Also, avoid `expr` for arithmetic; use `$(( ))`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Run `shellcheck` on your script; it catches most of these pitfalls automatically.
